summary: Chinese has no present tense — it has no tenses at all. The verb never changes: 我吃, 你吃, 他吃, 我们吃, 他们吃 — one form for every person and number, where German has ich esse, du isst, er isst. Whether something happens now, as a habit or later is shown by the situation and by time words (今天 ‘today’, 现在 ‘now’ — S14); a finished action or an experience gets an aspect particle, 了 or 过 (S14), not a past tense. So 我喝茶 is ‘I drink tea’, ‘I’m having tea’ or ‘I’ll have tea’ — whichever the moment makes clear.

blocks.title: No tense, only time
blocks.text: 我喝茶 can be ‘I drink tea’ (a habit), ‘I’m having tea’ (now) or ‘I’ll have tea’ (a plan). When it matters, a time word before the verb says when: 我今天喝茶 ‘I’m having tea today’ — the time words come in S14.

blocks.title: Aspect instead of tense (S14)
blocks.text: Where other languages use tenses, Chinese uses small particles: 了 for a completed action (我喝了茶 ‘I had the tea’), 过 for an experience (我喝过 ‘I have had it before’), 在 for an action in progress (我在喝茶 ‘I’m drinking tea’). They come in S14 with the days and the times of day.

items.title: German: the verb carries person and tense
points: ich trinke — du trinkst — er trinkt

items.title: Chinese: the verb is a bare word
points: 我喝 — 你喝 — 他喝
time and aspect = separate words: 今天, 了, 过

blocks.title: Nothing goes on the verb — and no 是
blocks.text: There is no ending for ‘he’ or ‘they’ (他喝, 他们喝), and 是 is not a helping verb: ‘I drink tea’ is 我喝茶, never *我是喝茶. 是 links nouns (S01).

askYourself: Who does it? → the subject comes first; the verb is the same for every person.
Now, a habit or a plan? → the same sentence; add a time word only if it is needed (S14).
Finished, or ever experienced? → that is aspect (了 / 过), not a tense — S14.
Did I put 是 before the verb? → take it out: 我喝茶.
steps: object — and a time word before the verb when needed (S14)

traps: Don’t look for an ending: 他喝 ‘he drinks’, 你们喝 ‘you drink’ — the same 喝.
*我是喝茶 for ‘I drink tea’ → 我喝茶.
Don’t look for a future tense either: ‘I’ll drink tea tomorrow’ is just 我明天喝茶 (a time word, S14).
了 is not a past tense ending to put on every verb: it marks completion or a change (S14).

quiz.why: The verb never changes and needs no 是.

quiz.q: Which form of 喝 goes with 我们 ‘we’?
quiz.why: One form for every person; 了 is aspect (S14), not agreement.

options: I drink tea / I’m having tea / I’ll have tea
only ‘I am drinking tea at this moment’
quiz.answer: I drink tea / I’m having tea / I’ll have tea
quiz.why: There is no tense: the situation (or a time word) decides.

quiz.q: How does Chinese say when something happens?
options: with time words before the verb (S14)
with a different form of the verb
quiz.answer: with time words before the verb (S14)
quiz.why: Time is a separate word, not a verb form.
Bare verb, no 是 — and 她们 would be ‘they’.

notes.text: Greek endings carry person, number, tense and aspect (τρώω, τρως, τρώει; έφαγα; θα φάω); Chinese 吃 never changes. θα for the future has no Chinese match: 我明天吃 needs only the time word.

Russian conjugates for person in the present (ем, ешь, ест) and for gender in the past (ел / ела); Chinese 吃 never changes. The Russian aspect pairs (есть / съесть) meet their Chinese counterparts in 了 and 过.
Spanish endings carry person and tense (como, comes, comí, comeré); Chinese 吃 stays the same and lets 我, 你 and time words do that work.
English verbs already change little (I eat, he eats), so Chinese is one step further: no -s, no -ed, no ‘will’. ‘I eat’ and ‘I’m eating’ can both be 我吃; ‘I ate’ is 我吃了, or just a time word.
French conjugation (je mange, nous mangeons, j’ai mangé, je mangerai) disappears entirely: 我吃 for every person and every time.
German conjugation (ich esse, du isst, er isst) and Präteritum, Perfekt, Futur have no Chinese counterpart: 吃 stays 吃, and time words and 了 / 过 do the work.
Hindi verbs change for gender, number, person and tense (खाता हूँ, खाती है, खाया); Chinese 吃 is one form for everyone and every time.
Persian endings show the person (mikhoram, mikhori, mikhorad) and prefixes the tense or mood (mi-, be-); Chinese 吃 never changes.
Marathi verbs change for person, gender, number and tense (खातो, खाते, खाल्ले); Chinese 吃 never changes.
Arabic verbs take prefixes and suffixes for person, number and gender (aktubu, taktubu, yaktubūna) and have two stems (kataba / yaktubu); a Chinese verb has one form.
Hebrew present forms change for gender and number (okhel, okhelet, okhlim), past and future for person; Chinese 吃 never changes.
Turkish stacks tense and person suffixes (yiyorum, yedim, yiyeceğim); Chinese has no suffixes at all: 我吃, 我吃了, 我明天吃.
Japanese verbs do not change for person (食べる for I, you, he) — like Chinese — but they do for tense and politeness (食べた, 食べます); Chinese 吃 changes for nothing.
Korean verbs do not change for person either, but their endings show tense and speech level (먹어요, 먹었어요); Chinese 吃 never changes.
Finnish conjugates for person and tense (syön, syöt, söin); Chinese 吃 is the same for everyone and every time.
Hungarian conjugates for person and tense and even shows whether the object is definite; Chinese 吃 never changes.
Swahili builds each verb from prefixes for person and tense (ninakula ‘I eat’, nilikula ‘I ate’, nitakula ‘I will eat’); Chinese 吃 has none: 我吃, 我吃了, 我明天吃.
Luganda verbs carry prefixes for person and tense (ndya ‘I eat’); Chinese 吃 carries nothing — 我, 昨天 and 了 do that work.
Vietnamese verbs never change either; optional words such as đã, đang, sẽ add time or aspect, as Chinese adds 了, 在 or a time word.
Inuktitut packs tense, person and much more into one verb word (nirijunga ‘I eat’); Chinese keeps everything separate and the verb unchanged: 我吃.

seeAlso.note: German conjugates: ich trinke, du trinkst, er trinkt, wir trinken, ihr trinkt, sie trinken — six forms where Chinese has one, 喝.
Arabic marks person, number and gender with prefixes and suffixes (أَشْرَبُ ‘I drink’, يَشْرَبُ ‘he drinks’, تَشْرَبُ ‘she drinks’); Chinese 喝 never changes.
The Hebrew present agrees in gender and number, not in person (שׁוֹתֶה, שׁוֹתָה, שׁוֹתִים, שׁוֹתוֹת); Chinese marks neither.
